design_detail: Randomized between-subjects balanced-placebo laboratory experiment, 2 × 2 × 2: beverage given (vodka and tonic, or tonic only) × instructions (told the drinks were vodka and tonic, or tonic only), with each of the four cells run in two non-randomized groups of men: 32 classified by the study as alcoholic from their history (treatment admissions, drunkenness arrests, Alcoholics Anonymous or a vocational rehabilitation programme for alcoholism; called here the alcoholism group) and 32 social drinkers. Drinking was measured during a 15-minute ad-lib 'taste-rating' task used as a cover story. Madison, Wisconsin; received December 1971, published 1973.
can_establish: Whether, in this short laboratory taste task, the belief that the drinks contained alcohol and the actual presence of alcohol each changed how much men with and without alcoholism drank in 15 minutes, at the modest blood-alcohol levels the task produced.
cannot_establish: Whether alcohol triggers uncontrolled drinking over longer periods, at higher blood-alcohol levels or outside a taste test (the authors name these limits, pp. 240–241); whether the alcoholism group's heavier drinking is caused by alcoholism (that comparison is not randomized and the groups differed in age and social class); whether a moderate pharmacological effect was missed (8 men per cell); or anything about women.

sample.recruitment: Community recruitment in and around Madison, Wisconsin. Alcoholism group: sign-up sheets left with hotel desk clerks and bartenders in areas the authors describe as frequented by people with alcoholism, inviting volunteers to a taste study that might involve sampling alcohol; names supplied by a former treatment patient of local people believed to be drinking again; and friends and acquaintances of these men. Social drinkers: the same sign-up sheets in hotels, bars, a university workplace and with taxi drivers, a newspaper advertisement for male social drinkers aged 21 or over, and friends of other participants. Paid five dollars; the consent form said alcohol might or might not be consumed (pp. 234–235).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All: men; a 30-minute screening interview on demographics, drinking pattern, treatment history and arrests for drunken conduct; candidates were not told the criteria for group assignment (p. 235). Alcoholism group: at least one of (a) one or more admissions to an alcoholism treatment centre, (b) five or more arrests for drunk and disorderly conduct, (c) past membership of Alcoholics Anonymous or the local vocational rehabilitation programme for alcoholism (all but 7 of 32 met two or more); and alcohol drunk within the previous 2 weeks with no immediate intention to stop, so that men trying to stay abstinent were not involved (p. 235). Social drinkers: did not abstain and did not meet the alcoholism criteria; excluded if they reported heavy drinking or called their drinking a problem (p. 235). Breath test on arrival: readings above 0.06% led to a new appointment; participants had been asked not to drink for 12 hours beforehand (p. 235). No diagnostic instrument was used.
sample.demographics: Alcoholism group: age 24–65 (mean 46.75); 23 had been treated for alcoholism (mean 5.5 admissions), 21 had drinking-related arrests (mean 21.5 arrests), 18 reported past Alcoholics Anonymous membership and 10 the vocational rehabilitation programme. Social drinkers: age 23–63 (mean 37.19); the age difference was significant (p < .01). Hollingshead social class index 59.2 vs 52.2, both within Social Class IV. Education (other than as part of the index), ethnicity, usual drinking quantity and other drug use are not reported (p. 235).
sample.attrition: None reported; the degrees of freedom of every analysis (1/56) fit complete data on 64 men in 8 cells. The numbers screened, rejected, or sent home after a positive breath test are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Men recruited through bars, hotels and a former patient's contacts who were currently drinking and not trying to abstain, compared with younger social drinkers recruited partly by newspaper advertisement; the groups differ in age (9.6 years on the printed means) and social class index, and the group comparison is not randomized. Excluding men who wanted to abstain means the results do not describe people in recovery. A taste-study invitation may have selected men willing to drink in a laboratory.

exposure.measurement: Manipulated. Beverage: vodka and tonic, or tonic only; instructions: told the beverage was vodka and tonic, or tonic only (four cells within each group). The alcoholic mixture was chosen in a pretest in which 25 student social drinkers could not tell it from tonic better than chance (44% judged it alcoholic) (p. 234). All participants rinsed with a mouthwash to which alcohol had been added, described as dulling taste and creating an alcohol sensation in the mouth (p. 236). Manipulation check: after the task each man was asked whether any drink had contained alcohol and, if yes, what percentage (p. 236). Blood alcohol was not measured after the task; for men given alcohol it was estimated from body weight and alcohol drunk with a published formula (American Medical Association, 1959) (pp. 237, 239).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions, oral: a primer drink about 20 minutes before the task (in the alcohol conditions described as equivalent to one bar mixed drink; tonic only in the others), then free access for 15 minutes to three decanters, with the instruction to sample as much as needed to rate the drinks (pp. 236–237). The amount drunk was self-selected. Mean estimated end-of-task blood alcohol: alcoholism group .093% (told alcohol) and .056% (told tonic); social drinkers .044% and .031% (p. 239).
exposure.polysubstance: Not assessed or reported (other drugs, tobacco).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Asked not to drink for 12 hours before the session; breath test on arrival, readings above 0.06% sent home to return sober; the authors state all but a few eligible men read zero (p. 235).

comparison.controls: For the randomized factors, the other beverage and instruction cells within the same group (8 men per cell, implied by the degrees of freedom). For the group factor, 32 male social drinkers.
comparison.matching: Age matching was attempted but failed (mean 46.75 vs 37.19 years, p < .01); age was not significantly correlated with any consumption measure (coefficients not printed, p. 239). Social class index 59.2 vs 52.2. No matching on usual drinking.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Usual quantity and frequency of drinking, tolerance, craving before the session, other drug use, smoking, psychiatric comorbidity and body weight (used for the blood-alcohol estimates) are not measured or not reported.

outcomes.instruments: (1) Total amount drunk in fluid ounces (the 72 ounces in the decanters minus what remained, allowing for the 6-ounce primer); (2) number of sips, counted in 3-minute blocks by a rater behind a disguised one-way mirror; (3) amount per sip (total divided by sips; an approximation by the authors' account); (4) post-task estimates of the percentage of alcohol in the drinks; plus formula-estimated blood alcohol in the given-alcohol cells and informal remarks heard over an intercom (pp. 236–237, 240).
outcomes.validity_norms: The taste-rating task adapts a procedure from a study of eating (Schachter, Goldman & Gordon, 1968); no validation of it as a measure of drinking is reported. The authors call the per-sip index and the per-block values of Figure 1 approximations (pp. 237–238).
outcomes.operationalization: Loss of control was operationalized as greater, and progressively increasing, drinking by men actually given alcohol, especially in the alcoholism group. The progressive-increase part was judged only by inspecting Figure 1 (3-minute blocks); no statistical test of the time course is reported (pp. 238–240).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four 2 × 2 × 2 fixed-effects analyses of variance (seven effects each, 28 F tests) plus correlations of age with each measure; only significant F values are printed.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The rater counting sips was unaware of the condition (p. 236). The experimenter (the second author) prepared the drinks in front of each participant, read the instructions and returned midway through the task, so she knew the assignment (p. 236).

analysis.effect_sizes: As printed (no standard deviations anywhere). Total amount: instructions F = 20.59, df = 1/56, p < .01 (told tonic 9.12 vs told alcohol 17.77 fl oz in the text; Table 1 gives 18.77); beverage F = .50 (given tonic 14.69 vs given alcohol 13.19); group F = 7.22, p < .01 (alcoholism group 16.80 vs social drinkers 11.08); interactions not significant, F not printed (p. 237). Sips: group F = 5.68, p < .025 (21.59 vs 29.81); beverage F = 4.01, p < .05 (alcohol 22.25 vs tonic 29.16) (p. 237). Amount per sip: group F = 10.65 (.92 vs .48 oz) and instructions F = 11.89 (.94 vs .46 oz), both p < .01 (p. 238). Alcohol-content estimates: instructions F = 44.49, p < .01 (about 1% vs 27.6%) (p. 239). Editors' calculations (from the printed means and F ratios, 32 men per level, df 56): the three F ratios for total amount imply the same within-cell SD of about 8.5 fl oz (8.46 to 8.52); instructions d ≈ 1.13 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.64); beverage d ≈ −0.18 (95% CI −0.68 to 0.33; difference −1.5 oz, 95% CI −5.8 to +2.8); within the alcoholism group, given alcohol minus given tonic −1.2 oz (95% CI −7.2 to +4.8; 16 vs 16 men); group d ≈ 0.67; group × instructions F(1,56) ≈ 1.7, p ≈ .20 (instruction effect 12.4 oz in the alcoholism group, 6.9 oz in social drinkers); within the told-alcohol cells, alcoholism group minus social drinkers 8.5 oz, t(56) ≈ 2.8, p ≈ .007. Within-cell SDs implied for sips about 13.8 and for amount per sip about 0.55 oz.
analysis.covariates: None; age was correlated with the dependent measures instead of being adjusted for (p. 239).
analysis.selective_reporting: No standard deviations, standard errors or mean squares; cell sizes not printed; non-significant F values omitted, including the group × instructions interaction that bears on the discussion's claim about the alcoholism group; the time course in Figure 1 is described but not tested.
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 8 men per cell, the editors' 95% interval for the effect of alcohol on total amount runs from about two-thirds of a standard deviation less to one-third more, so a moderate pharmacological effect cannot be excluded.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 64 men in a 15-minute laboratory taste test, being told the drinks contained vodka roughly doubled the amount drunk (about 18.8 vs 9.1 fl oz from Table 1; editors' d ≈ 1.1), while actually receiving vodka made no detectable difference (13.2 vs 14.7 oz), in both groups. The alcoholism group drank more overall and in larger sips but sipped less often; drinking mostly fell across the session; estimated end-of-task blood alcohol averaged .031% to .093%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports these results accurately and says loss of control did not occur during the task. The discussion calls the findings opposed to the view that alcohol's physiological effects alone drive increased drinking, and "strong support for the role of cognitive factors" in loss of control (p. 240). It also states that the alcoholism group told alcohol drank significantly more than the social drinkers and attributes this to a greater expectation of reinforcing effects (p. 240); no such test is printed (an editors' simple-effect test would probably support the difference), the group × instructions interaction was not significant, and expectation of reinforcement was not measured. The same discussion names the limits that restrict the inference (a short task, blood alcohol below the level at which loss of control may begin, demand characteristics of a taste test) and closes by saying the study does not discount physiological factors (pp. 240–241). The null effect of alcohol rests on 8 men per cell and is imprecise.

timeline.event: Engle & Williams, effect of an ounce of vodka on desire for alcohol in people with alcoholism (as titled in Hull & Bond's reference list); reanalysed in balanced-placebo form by Maisto, Lauerman & Adesso (1977), according to Hull & Bond (1986, p. 354).
This experiment: told-alcohol instructions, not alcohol itself, increased drinking in a 15-minute taste task in men with and without alcoholism.
Maisto, Lauerman & Adesso: expectancy g 0.52, alcohol effect not significant, as coded by Hull & Bond (1986, Table 9); primary paper not read.

Berg, LaBerg, Skutle & Ohman, instructed versus pharmacological effects of alcohol in alcoholics and social drinkers (title as listed): expectancy g 0.39, alcohol g 0.05, as coded by Hull & Bond (1986, Table 9); primary paper not read.

Hull & Bond meta-analysis: across these three studies of drinking or desire to drink, expectancy g 0.523 (Z = 2.870, p < .01) and alcohol g −0.040. It codes this experiment as expectancy g 0.66 and alcohol g −0.17, values the editors reproduce by averaging total amount, sip count and amount per sip, so 0.66 understates the expectancy effect on the amount drunk (about 1.1).
Testa et al., symposium report revisiting the placebo condition in alcohol expectancy research; on the project's General list, not yet appraised.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the finding (expectancy, not alcohol content, raised drinking) was seen in all three balanced-placebo studies of drinking or desire to drink pooled by Hull & Bond (1986), who do not report their doses, session lengths or settings. This experiment speaks against alcohol at low doses triggering escalating drinking within a short laboratory task; it does not test loss of control at higher blood alcohol, over longer periods or in natural settings, the limits the authors themselves named.

funding.funder: Supported in part by Grant MH-17982 from the National Institutes of Mental Health to the senior author (footnote 1, p. 233; funder's name as printed).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the University of Wisconsin for the study; the first author had moved to the University of Washington and the third to the Oregon Research Institute (footnotes 2 and 3, p. 233). The second author was the experimenter who prepared the drinks and gave the instructions (p. 236). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A balanced-placebo or placebo-controlled experiment in people with alcohol use disorder diagnosed with a standard instrument, women included, with longer self-paced access in a more natural setting, blood alcohol measured rather than estimated across a range of levels under medical supervision, craving rated before and after the first drink, drinks prepared and instructions given by staff blind to the beverage, and enough participants to estimate the alcohol × group interaction with a useful confidence interval.

domains.note: Participants were randomly assigned to the four cells within each group, but sequence generation, allocation concealment and baseline characteristics by cell are not reported. The group factor (alcoholism group vs social drinkers) is not randomized and lies outside RoB 2: it is confounded by age, social class and recruitment route.

The experimenter knew each assignment and interacted with the participant (instructions, a midway check). The alcohol-laced mouthwash given to everyone may have weakened the told-tonic instructions. The manipulation check suggests the deception held: men told tonic but given alcohol estimated 0% (alcoholism group) and 3.5% (social drinkers) alcohol.
Complete data implied for all 64 men (df 1/56 in every analysis).
Amount drunk was measured as volume left in the decanters; sips were counted by a rater unaware of the condition. The secondary blood-alcohol values were estimated by formula, not measured.
No protocol (1973). All four measures are reported, but without standard deviations and with non-significant F values omitted; the time-course hypothesis was judged from a figure without a test.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applies to the randomized comparisons (instructions and beverage). Their main outcome, volume drunk, is objective and complete, so the instruction effect is credible within this task; concerns come from unreported randomization details, an experimenter who knew the assignment and dealt with participants, and incomplete statistical reporting. The comparison of the alcoholism group with social drinkers is observational and confounded by age, social class and recruitment, and is citable only as a descriptive difference. The null effect of alcohol is imprecise (8 men per cell). Citable for: in a 15-minute laboratory taste task at low estimated blood alcohol, what men with and without alcoholism believed they were drinking, not what they drank, determined how much they drank. Not citable for: absence of loss of control at higher doses, over longer periods or in natural settings, or for women.

key_findings.finding: Being told the drinks contained vodka increased the total amount drunk in 15 minutes: 9.12 fl oz in the told-tonic cells vs 17.77 fl oz (as printed in the text) in the told-alcohol cells, F = 20.59, df = 1/56, p < .01, in both groups.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amount of Beverage Consumed, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: Table 1 implies 18.77, not 17.77, for the told-alcohol mean ((23.00 + 14.53)/2; also twice the grand mean 13.94 minus 9.12). Editors' calculation: d ≈ 1.13 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.64), using the within-cell SD of about 8.5 oz implied by the printed F ratios.

key_findings.finding: The beverage actually given did not change the amount drunk: 14.69 fl oz when given tonic vs 13.19 when given vodka and tonic, F = .50, df = 1/56; the instructions × beverage interaction was not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amount of Beverage Consumed, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: difference −1.5 oz (95% CI −5.8 to +2.8), d ≈ −0.18 (−0.68 to 0.33); within the alcoholism group alone −1.2 oz (95% CI −7.2 to +4.8), 16 vs 16 men.

key_findings.finding: Cell means for total amount drunk: alcoholism group told tonic 10.94 (given tonic) and 10.25 (given alcohol), told alcohol 23.87 and 22.13; social drinkers told tonic 9.31 and 5.94, told alcohol 14.62 and 14.44 fl oz; grand mean 13.94.
The alcoholism group drank more than the social drinkers overall (16.80 vs 11.08 fl oz, F = 7.22, df = 1/56, p < .01); the group × instructions interaction is reported only as not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amount of Beverage Consumed, 1st paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1: the instruction effect was 12.4 oz in the alcoholism group and 6.9 oz in social drinkers, interaction F(1,56) ≈ 1.7, p ≈ .20. The group comparison is not randomized; the groups differ in age and social class.

key_findings.finding: Sips: social drinkers took more sips than the alcoholism group (29.81 vs 21.59, F = 5.68, df = 1/56, p < .025), and all men sipped more often when given tonic than when given vodka and tonic (29.16 vs 22.25, F = 4.01, p < .05); instructions and interactions were not significant.

Amount per sip: the alcoholism group drank more per sip than social drinkers (.92 vs .48 fl oz, F = 10.65, df = 1/56, p < .01), and men told alcohol drank more per sip than men told tonic (.94 vs .46 fl oz, F = 11.89, p < .01); the beverage given and the interactions were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amount Consumed Per Sip, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Post-task estimates of alcohol content depended only on the instructions (F = 44.49, df = 1/56, p < .01): about 1% in the told-tonic cells vs 27.6% in the told-alcohol cells. Told and given alcohol: 21.3% (alcoholism group) and 23.1% (social drinkers); told alcohol but given tonic: 28.7% and 37.2%; told tonic but given alcohol: 0% and 3.5%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Estimates of Alcohol Content, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Estimated end-of-task blood alcohol (formula from weight and alcohol drunk; not measured) in the given-alcohol cells: alcoholism group .093% (told alcohol) and .056% (told tonic); social drinkers .044% and .031%. The authors place the alcoholism group within, and the social drinkers below, a borderline-intoxication range of .05% to .15%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Postexperimental Blood-Alcohol Concentrations, 1st paragraph (continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: A pen mark in the scan crosses the last digit of .056; it reads as 6 on a high-resolution crop (the text layer gives .055).

key_findings.finding: Drinking did not rise progressively in men given alcohol: in most cells consumption was highest in the first 3-minute block and fell over the remaining 12 minutes; the exception the authors name is the social drinkers told tonic but given alcohol, whose drinking stayed low and stable.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (p. 238); Results › Amount Consumed Per Sip, 2nd paragraph (p. 238, continuing on p. 239); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 240)
key_findings.note: No test of the time course is reported, and the authors call the per-block values approximations. Editors' reading of Figure 1 on a high-resolution crop (approximate): in the alcoholism group told and given alcohol, about 7.9 oz in the first block falling to about 2.0 in the fourth, then about 2.9 in the last.

key_findings.finding: Age was not significantly correlated with any consumption measure (coefficients not printed), which the authors take to show that the age gap between the groups did not drive drinking.

Informal observation only: several men told alcohol but given tonic, in both groups, volunteered that they felt a buzz or a bit tipsy; no systematic measure of intoxication or craving was taken, and the authors propose such measures for future work.

The authors list limits to generalizing: the task may have been too short; loss of control may begin only above the blood-alcohol levels reached; the taste-test framing may have discouraged drinking, since participants may have thought intoxication would spoil their ratings. They propose longer sessions, instructions encouraging heavy drinking and observation in natural drinking settings, and say the study does not discount physiological factors.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 240, right column) and 5th–6th paragraphs (pp. 240–241)

key_findings.finding: Participants: 32 men classified as alcoholic from their history (all but 7 meeting two or more criteria; 23 with treatment admissions, mean 5.5; 21 with drinking-related arrests, mean 21.5; 18 past Alcoholics Anonymous members) who had drunk in the past 2 weeks and did not intend to stop, and 32 male social drinkers; mean age 46.75 vs 37.19 years (p < .01); social class index 59.2 vs 52.2.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the told-alcohol mean for total amount drunk as 17.77 fl oz, but Table 1 implies a different value (condition means 23.00 and 14.53; grand mean 13.94 with the told-tonic mean 9.12); editors' arithmetic: 18.77 from the condition means, 18.76 from the grand mean.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error in the text; the table value (about 18.8 oz) should be cited, which makes the instruction effect slightly larger than the text states.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion of age describes the alcoholism group as on average 6 years older (p. 239), but the printed means (46.75 and 37.19 years, p. 235) differ by more (editors' arithmetic: 9.6 years).
reporting_issues.consequence: The groups differed in age more than the age check says; that check (no significant correlation of age with the drinking measures) prints no coefficients and cannot be weighed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say up to 72 fluid ounces were available during the 15-minute task, but the Method states that the 6-ounce primer was drawn from the same three decanters (2 ounces from each) and allowed for in the total.
reporting_issues.consequence: About 66 ounces were available during the task. No cell mean approached either limit (highest 23.87), so the comparisons are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: No standard deviations, standard errors or mean squares are reported, cell sizes are not printed (8 per cell is implied by df 1/56), and non-significant F values are omitted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes and intervals must be back-calculated. The within-cell SD for total amount implied by the three printed F ratios (instructions, group, beverage) is the same, about 8.5 oz (editors' calculation), which supports the internal consistency of the printed means and F values.

reporting_issues.issue: The four estimated blood-alcohol means are not proportional to the amounts drunk in the same cells of Table 1: per fluid ounce of beverage, about .0042% and .0055% in the alcoholism group and .0030% and .0052% in social drinkers (editors' arithmetic); body weights and the inputs to the formula are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimates cannot be checked, and they were estimated rather than measured; the authors' suggestion that blood alcohol stayed below the level at which loss of control might begin rests on them.

reporting_issues.issue: The text summarizes Figure 1 as highest drinking in the first block and decline afterwards, with one exception, but the figure also shows rises in two alcoholism-group cells; editors' approximate reading: told and given alcohol, about 2.0 to 2.9 oz in the last 3-minute block; told tonic but given alcohol, about 3.1 to 3.5 oz from the first to the second block.
reporting_issues.consequence: Single-block fluctuations in 8 men, not the progressive increase the authors looked for; the narrative is smoother than the figure, and no statistical test of the time course was made.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, scanned), J Abnorm Psychol 81(3): 233–241, pp. 233–241 (all pages, including footnotes and references). The text layer is a poor OCR, so every number was read on the pages rendered at 150 dpi; Tables 1–4 and the subject and blood-alcohol paragraphs checked on 300- and 600-dpi crops; Figure 1 read at 600 dpi, values from it labelled approximate. Handwritten underlining in the scan crosses some words and one digit (noted). The text layer misreads several values that are correct on the rendered pages (for example 9.31 as 0.31 in Table 1, 21.59 as 21.55, 5.5 admissions as 5.S, 18 as IS, 52.2 as 52,2, df 1/56 as 1/S6 on p. 239, .056 as .055), so the rendered page is the source.
